About
Sendoku %1$s
A sudoku app for people who have run out of hard sudoku.
No advertisements
Not between puzzles, not for hints, not ever.
No tracking
Nothing is measured and nothing is sent. There is no server.
No purchases
Every puzzle and every hint is here already.
Works offline
The whole batch ships inside the app.
Hints that teach
A hint names the technique and explains the reasoning. It never just fills in a digit, and it is never sold: three come with every puzzle, and you can turn the limit off in settings.
Difficulty is rated by the hardest technique a puzzle actually needs, worked out by solving it the way a person would. That is why a Severe here means the same thing as the last Severe.

The box has to hold this digit somewhere, and every place it could go lies on one line. So the digit is on that line, and it cannot be anywhere else along it.

Those two cells will take those two digits between them, one each. No other cell in the region can have either.
The region needs both digits, and only these two cells can take them, so they take one each. Everything else in those two cells is out.

Each of the two rows needs the digit once, and both can only place it in the same two columns. Between them they use up both columns, so no other row can have the digit there.
Three rows needing the digit, and only three columns to put it in. The three rows use up all three columns, so nothing else in those columns can have it.
Four rows and four columns, the same argument again. The four rows fill all four columns between them.
The middle cell is one of its two digits. Either way, one of the two outer cells is forced to the shared digit, so anything seeing both of them cannot be it.
The middle cell can also be the shared digit, so the conclusion is weaker: only a cell that sees all three loses it.
If neither of the pair cells took the second digit, both would take the first, and the linked region would have nowhere left to put it. So one of them is the second digit.

Colour the chain alternately and exactly one colour is true. Either a colour lands twice in one region and is therefore false, or a cell outside sees both colours and loses the digit whichever way it falls.
One colour of the first chain clashes with a colour of the second, which forces the digit into one of the two opposite colours. Anything seeing both of those cannot hold it.
Neighbours in the chain see each other, so they alternate. The two ends are an odd number of steps apart and therefore hold one digit each, and anything seeing both can have neither.
If those four cells held nothing but the same two digits, they could be swapped around the rectangle and the puzzle would have two answers. It has one, so that arrangement is impossible.

If the extra candidate were removed, every digit would appear exactly twice in every region, and a grid like that always has an even number of answers. This puzzle has one, so the extra candidate is the answer.
The chain alternates between places the digit must be and places it cannot be. The two ends cannot both be empty of it, so anything seeing both loses it.
Suppose the first cell is not the digit. Follow the chain along and the last cell is forced to be it. So one end or the other holds it.

Follow both possibilities. If one of them leaves a cell with nothing to put in it, that possibility was never real and can go. If both of them put the same digit in the same place, that digit belongs there whichever one turns out to be true. Nothing here depends on the assumption being right, which is what makes it a proof and not a guess.

Whatever the cell turns out to be, it knocks its own digit out of the matching group, and that group is then full and must use every digit it has left. If all the groups hold the same spare digit, that digit lands in one of them no matter which way the cell falls. Anything that can see it in all of them loses it.

If the digit under threat is gone from the first group, that group is full and must take the digit it shares with the middle one. The middle group then loses that digit, so it is full too and takes the digit it shares with the third. The third group is then full as well, and has to use the digit under threat. So any cell that can see it in both outer groups cannot have it.

The shared cells will use up all but two of their digits, and the two groups either side claim exactly those two. So every digit of the group in the line is spent inside the line, and every digit of the group in the box is spent inside the box. Nothing else in either one can have them.
One shared digit can only appear in one of the two groups, which locks the other group and forces it to use every digit it has. So the second shared digit lands in one group or the other.

What a sudoku is
Every row, every column and every box holds each digit once.
This is a sudoku. A small one, four cells by four, so everything fits in your head at once. The full size grid works exactly the same way.
This is a row. It has to hold the digits 1, 2, 3 and 4, each of them once. No repeats, and nothing left out.
This is a column. Same rule: 1, 2, 3 and 4, each of them once.
That is the whole game. There is no arithmetic in it, and nothing to add up. It is one rule about where a digit is allowed to be.
These two cells are empty. Filling them in so the rule still holds is what solving means.
Rows, columns and boxes
A cell sits in three houses at once, and shares a rule with all of them.
The rule mentioned rows and columns. There is a third kind of group, and it is the one that makes a sudoku worth solving.
Here is a row again.
Here is a column.
And here is a box, marked by the heavier lines. It holds each digit once too.

So this cell belongs to three groups at the same time. Every cell it shares a group with is lit up, and none of them can hold the same digit it does. Those three groups are called houses, and the word is used from here on.
Givens
The digits printed at the start are fixed, and they are what makes the answer the only one.
These digits came with the puzzle. They are called givens, and they cannot be changed or erased.
They are drawn differently from the digits you place, so you can always tell which is which. In this app the givens are the heavier ones.
These are the cells you fill in.

A properly made puzzle has exactly one way to fill them. That is a promise about the puzzle, not about you: if you are stuck, there is still only one answer, and it can always be reasoned out. Every puzzle in this app is made that way.
Your first solve
Look at what a cell cannot be, and sometimes only one digit is left.
Now solve one. Two cells are empty, and the rule is enough to fill both.
Start with this row. It already has a 1 and a 4, so the two empty cells hold 2 and 3 between them. The question is which way round.
This cell cannot be 2, because its column already has one. So it is 3.
That leaves one empty cell, and one digit unused in the row.
Your turn. Place the digit that belongs here.
Not quite. Look at the row: which digit from 1 to 4 is still missing from it?
Solved. That is a sudoku, whatever the size of the grid.
A bigger grid
Boxes are not always square, and the rule does not care.
Six by six. The rule has not changed, but the boxes have: they are three wide and two tall.
This is one box. Three across, two down, six cells, each digit from 1 to 6 once.
That catches people out at first, because the eye expects a square. It is worth a moment: find the box that this cell is in before you look for anything else.
Your turn. One digit is missing from the top left box.
Not that one. Count what the box already holds, then find the digit from 1 to 6 that is not there.
Good. From here on the grids are nine by nine and the boxes are square again, but the habit of checking all three houses is the one to keep.
The naked single
A cell with only one digit left has to hold it.
A full size grid, and the first technique with a name. It is the simplest one there is, and even on the hardest puzzles it is what finishes most cells.
Look at this cell on its own. Ask what it could hold.
Every cell that rules something out is lit. Between its row, its column and its box, eight of the nine digits already appear somewhere it can see.
So one digit is left, and the cell has to hold it. Nothing else is possible. That is a naked single: naked because you can see it by looking at one cell, single because one digit survives.
The app calls this by name when it gives you a hint. Now you know what it means.
The hidden single
A digit with only one place left in a house has to go there.
The other kind of single, and the one that finds more cells. A naked single is a cell with one digit left. This is the mirror image: a digit with one cell left.
Take a house, and pick a digit it still needs. Ask where in that house the digit could go.
In this box the answer is one cell. Every other empty cell in the box is ruled out by its own row or column.
So the digit goes there, even though that cell has several digits it could hold on its own. That is why it is called hidden: the digit is hiding among the others.
This is the one worth learning properly. On most puzzles it is what keeps you moving after the naked singles run out.
Your turn. Place the digit that has nowhere else to go in this box.
Not that one. Ask which digit the box still needs, then check where each of them could actually fit.
How to look
Sweep a digit across the grid instead of studying cells one at a time.
You now know two techniques. Knowing them is not the same as finding them, and finding them is what takes the time.
Do not read the grid cell by cell. Take one digit, say the one that appears most often already, and look at the three boxes in a band.
For each box ask a single question: where can this digit go? Rows and columns that already hold it cross out most of the answers, and often only one cell is left.
Then move to the next band, and when the digit is exhausted, move to the next digit. That is scanning, and it is what fast solvers are doing when they look like they are just staring.
It costs nothing to be systematic and it saves the feeling of being stuck, which is usually the feeling of having looked at the same corner four times.
A full grid, singles only
Everything you have learned so far is enough to finish a whole puzzle.
A real nine by nine, at the Gentle grade. Every step in it is a single, naked or hidden, and there is nothing here you have not met.
Here is one to start you off. This cell has eight of the nine digits ruled out by what it can see.
That is the shape of a Gentle puzzle. Singles, all the way to the end, and no guessing at any point.
When you leave this lesson, play one. The next stage is about notes, and notes only start to earn their keep on puzzles harder than this.
Your turn. One digit is possible here.
Look again at the row, the column and the box this cell is in, and list what they already hold.
Notes
A note is a record of what you worked out, so you do not have to work it out again.
From here on the puzzles stop yielding to singles, and you will need to write things down. A note, or pencil mark, is a small digit in a cell saying that digit is still possible there.
Look at this cell. Working out that it can only be one of two digits takes a few seconds. Writing those two digits in means it takes no seconds the next time you look.
That is all a note is. It is not a guess and it is not a commitment. It is a record of a deduction you already made.
Every technique from here on is about patterns in the notes rather than patterns in the digits. Pairs, triples, fish and chains are all read off the notes.
Nobody solves a hard sudoku in their head, and a solver who writes nothing down on a Diabolical is not being clever, they are being slow.
When to write them
Fill in notes when the singles run out, not before.
There are two ways to use notes, and the difference matters.

The first is to fill every empty cell with every possible digit, all at once, before doing anything else. It is thorough, it takes several minutes by hand, and on an easy puzzle most of it is wasted because singles would have finished the grid anyway.
The second is to mark only where you are working. These four cells are worth marking because something is going on among them. The rest of the grid is not.

The honest advice: solve the singles first, and start marking when you stop finding them. On paper that saves real time. In this app, filling every note is one tap, so the cost is smaller, but a grid full of numbers is still harder to read than a grid with notes only where they matter.
Keeping notes honest
A note that is out of date is worse than no note at all.
Notes have one danger. Every digit you place makes some of them wrong, and a wrong note will send you down an argument that cannot be right.
Place a digit here, and every cell it can see loses that digit as a possibility. If those notes are not rubbed out, the next technique you spot might be built on one of them.
This app can do it for you. There is a setting called rub out notes that a placement rules out, and it is on by default. On paper you do it by hand, and it is where most mistakes come from.
When a puzzle goes wrong and you cannot see why, a stale note is the first thing to suspect. The hint button will tell you when a digit you have placed cannot be right.
The pointing pair
If a digit in a box is stuck on one line, it leaves that line everywhere else.

The first technique that removes possibilities rather than placing a digit. Most techniques from here on do that, and it takes some getting used to: you make progress without writing a single digit in.
Look at where one digit can go in this box. Every place it could sit lies on the same column.
The box has to contain that digit somewhere. So wherever it ends up, it is in that column.
Which means the rest of the column cannot have it. These cells lose that digit as a possibility, even though they are nowhere near the box.
It is called pointing because the pair inside the box points along the line and clears it.
The claiming pair
If a digit on a line is stuck in one box, it leaves that box everywhere else.
The same argument read the other way round, and worth doing separately because the eye finds it in a different place.
This time start with a line. Look at where one digit can go along this row.
Every place it could sit is inside the same box. The row must hold that digit somewhere, so the digit is in that box.
Which means the rest of the box loses it. These cells cannot hold it any more.
Pointing looks at a box and clears a line. Claiming looks at a line and clears a box. Two names, one idea, and you will see both in every hard puzzle.
The naked pair
Two cells holding the same two digits own them both.
Now the groups. This is the smallest of them and the pattern that makes the rest obvious.
These two cells are in the same house, and each of them can only be one of the same two digits.
Between them they will take both of those digits, one each. Which is which does not matter and you do not need to know.
So no other cell in that house can hold either digit. This cell loses one of them.
Naked, again, because you can see it by reading the two cells. Nothing is hidden and no other cell is involved in the argument.
The hidden pair
Two digits with only the same two places left own those cells.
The mirror image of the naked pair, exactly as the hidden single mirrors the naked one.
In this house, two digits can each only go in the same two cells.
Those two digits will take those two cells between them. So whatever else those cells looked like they could hold, they cannot.
The two cells lose every other note. They are now a naked pair, and often that is what the pattern is for: turning a hidden pair into a naked one that clears the rest of the house.
Hidden pairs are harder to see than naked ones because you have to look at digits rather than cells. It is worth the effort on a grid that has stalled.
The naked triple
Three cells sharing three digits own them, even if none holds all three.
A pair with one more cell, and one wrinkle that catches everybody the first time.
These three cells sit in the same house, and between them they use only three different digits.
Here is the wrinkle: not one of them has to hold all three. Two digits in one cell, two in the next, two in the third is a triple, as long as only three digits appear across all of them.
The three cells will take the three digits between them, so every other cell in the house loses all three. That is a lot of notes gone at once.
When you are hunting, count the distinct digits across two or three cells rather than looking for identical notes. That is the habit that finds triples.
The hidden triple
Three digits with only three places left own those cells.
The same relationship as the hidden pair, one size up, and genuinely hard to spot.
In this house, three digits can only go in the same three cells between them.
So those three cells hold those three digits, and every other note in them can go.
Do not hunt for these first. Look for them when a house has several cells left and nothing else has worked. Most of the time a naked pattern in the same house is easier to see.
Quads
The same idea again with four, and worth knowing but rarely worth hunting.
Pairs, triples, and now quads. The argument does not change: four cells that between them use four digits own those digits, and four digits with only four places own those cells.
Here is a naked quad. Four cells, four digits between them, and the rest of the house loses all four.

And here is the honest advice. Quads are real and they are legal, but they are rare, and a quad in a house of five or six empty cells usually means there is a simpler pattern in the other cells that you have missed.
Here is a hidden quad, for completeness. Four digits with four places left.
Learn to recognise them so a hint naming one makes sense. Do not spend your time searching for them.
The X-Wing
A digit fixed to two columns in two rows leaves those columns everywhere else.
The first pattern that spans the whole grid rather than sitting inside one house. It has a shape, and once you have seen the shape you will see it everywhere.
Take one digit. In these two rows, it can only go in two cells each, and those cells are in the same two columns. Four cells, in a rectangle.
Now think it through. Each row must hold the digit once. Whichever corner one row uses, the other row must use the opposite one. There is no third option.
So between them, the two rows take that digit in both of those columns. Anything else in those columns loses it.
It works with columns and rows swapped too. Two columns whose digit is confined to the same two rows clears those rows.
The Swordfish
The same argument as an X-Wing, with three lines instead of two.
An X-Wing with a row added. The name is unhelpful but the pattern is a direct extension.
Three rows, one digit, and in each row that digit is confined to cells in the same three columns.
Not every row has to use all three columns. Two of the three is enough, as long as no row strays outside them.
The three rows take the digit in those three columns between them, so the rest of those columns loses it.
If you can follow the X-Wing you can follow this. Finding it is another matter: this is the point where filling in your notes stops being optional.
The Jellyfish
Four lines. The same pattern again, and the last one worth learning.
Four rows, one digit, four columns. The argument has not changed since the X-Wing and it will not change again.
Here is one. Four rows, and the digit in each is confined to the same four columns.

Beyond four there is nothing to learn. A five line version exists in theory, but on a nine by nine grid every one of them can be found as a smaller pattern in the four columns left over, so nobody looks for them.
This is the far edge of what is worth hunting by pattern. Past here, chains are a better use of your attention.
The XY-Wing
Three cells of two digits each, and one cell that loses out whichever way it goes.
The wings need a different way of thinking. Up to now you have found a pattern and read off a conclusion. Here you argue by cases.
Start with this cell. It holds exactly two possible digits, and it is the hinge of the pattern.
It has two friends, each sharing a house with it, and each holding two digits: one shared with the hinge, one shared with each other.

Now the argument. The hinge is one of its two digits. If it is the first, the left wing is forced to the shared digit. If it is the second, the right wing is forced to the same shared digit. Either way, one of the wings holds it.
So any cell that can see both wings cannot hold that digit. This one loses it.
You never learn what the hinge actually is. That is the point, and it is what makes wings feel different from everything before them.
The XYZ-Wing
Like an XY-Wing, but the hinge can be the shared digit too, so the conclusion is weaker.
One change to the XY-Wing, and it makes the conclusion smaller.
Here the hinge holds three digits rather than two, and the shared digit is one of them.
So now there are three cases, not two. Either wing might hold the shared digit, or the hinge itself might.
That means a cell only loses the digit if it can see all three, not just the two wings. Fewer cells qualify, which is why this pattern eliminates less than its simpler cousin.
Worth knowing because the shape looks almost identical, and reading it as an XY-Wing would let you eliminate a digit you are not entitled to.
The W-Wing
Two identical pairs joined by a line that must hold one of their digits.
The third wing, and the one that needs the least arithmetic.
Two cells, not sharing a house, each holding the same two digits.
Now find a house where one of those two digits can only go in two places, and those two places each see one of the pair cells. That house is the link.
The link house must hold that digit in one of its two places, and whichever it is, it forces one of the pair cells to take the other digit. So one of the pair holds the other digit, always.
Any cell seeing both pair cells loses it. This one does.
The unique rectangle
A puzzle with one answer cannot contain a square that could rotate.
This technique is different in kind from every other one, and it is worth saying why before using it.
Look at these four cells. They sit in two rows, two columns and exactly two boxes, and each of them can hold the same two digits.
If that were the whole story, the puzzle would have two answers: fill the rectangle one way, or swap both diagonals, and both grids obey every rule. A properly made puzzle does not have two answers.
So it cannot be the whole story. One of those cells has to hold something else, and that is what lets you eliminate.
Here the extra possibilities survive and the shared pair is struck from these cells.

The catch, stated plainly: this argument assumes the puzzle is well made. It is true of every puzzle in this app, because the generator checks. Use it on a grid from an unknown source and it can mislead you.
BUG plus one
If every cell but one had two candidates, the puzzle would be ambiguous. So that one is special.
The same assumption as the unique rectangle, wearing a different shape.
Suppose a grid reached a position where every unsolved cell held exactly two possibilities, and every digit appeared exactly twice in every house. Such a grid always has two answers.

So a properly made puzzle can never reach it. If you find a position that is one cell away, where exactly one cell holds three possibilities instead of two, that cell is what saves the puzzle from being ambiguous.
The digit that appears three times in its houses is the one it must hold. It is a rare pattern and a very fast finish when it turns up.
Simple colouring
Follow one digit through the cells where it has only two homes, and look for a contradiction.
Chains, gently. Colouring is the easiest way into them and the same reasoning underneath.
Pick a digit. Find a house where it has only two possible cells. Those two are linked: exactly one of them is the digit.
Colour one of the pair, then follow the links. Every cell connected this way ends up one of two colours, and one whole colour is right while the other is wrong. You do not know which.
Now look for the contradiction. If a cell can see two cells of the same colour, that colour cannot be the right one, so the cell loses the digit. Here that is what happens.
Two colours, one contradiction, and no guessing anywhere in it. That is the whole method.
Remote pairs
A chain of identical pairs alternates, so the ends are opposites.
Colouring applied to cells rather than to a single digit.
Here is a chain of cells that all hold the same two digits, each linked to the next by a shared house.
Because each link is a pair, the digits alternate along the chain. First cell takes one, second takes the other, and so on.
So the two ends of an even length chain are opposites: they hold different digits. Any cell that can see both ends must lose both digits, because one of the ends holds each.
It is the easiest chain to spot, because every cell in it looks the same.
Multi colouring
Two colouring chains that interact rule each other out.
Simple colouring uses one chain. Sometimes one chain has no contradiction in it but two chains together do.
Here are cells from two separate chains for the same digit.
If a colour in one chain sees a colour in the other, then those two colours cannot both be right. Following that through eliminates the digit from cells that see the two colours left over.
The conclusion lands here.
This is where colouring stops being something you can hold in your head and starts wanting a written note of which cell is which colour.
The X-Chain
One digit, links that alternate between strong and weak, and an elimination at the ends.
The general form of everything in the last stage. One digit, and a chain of alternating links.

A strong link is two cells where at least one must hold the digit, which is what a house with only two places gives you. A weak link is two cells where at most one can, which is any two cells sharing a house.
Alternate them: strong, weak, strong, and so on, starting and ending with strong. Then whatever happens in the middle, one of the two ends holds the digit.
So any cell seeing both ends loses it.
Colouring is this chain drawn in two colours. The chain is more general because it can pass through cells colouring cannot reach.
The XY-Chain
A chain of two candidate cells, where the ends share a digit.
The same alternating idea, but stepping through cells rather than following one digit.
Every cell in this chain holds exactly two possibilities, and each shares a house with the next.
Within a cell, taking one digit forces the other, which is the strong link. Between cells, a shared house makes the weak one. Alternating them runs the argument along the chain.
If both ends of the chain can hold the same digit, then one of them does, whichever way the chain falls. Any cell seeing both ends loses that digit.
This is the technique that finishes most Diabolical puzzles, and finding one is mostly a matter of following bivalue cells patiently rather than being clever.
Writing a chain down
A chain you cannot check is a guess with extra steps.
One practical lesson before the last technique, because chains are where people convince themselves of things that are not true.
A chain is a sequence of claims, and each one has to hold. On screen it looks like a set of highlighted cells, and highlighting is not an argument.
Write it as a line: this cell is either 4 or 7; if it is 4 then that one is 9; if that one is 9 then this other one is 4. Each arrow is a link and each link has a reason.
Then check the alternation. Strong, weak, strong, weak, and strong at both ends. A chain that starts or ends on a weak link proves nothing, and that is the most common way a chain goes wrong.
If you cannot write it down, you have not found it. That is not a rule about tidiness, it is the difference between a deduction and a hunch.
Sue de Coq
Where a box crosses a line, and the crossing has more digits than room.
A box and a column overlap in three cells. Those three cells belong to both at once, and that is what this technique lives on.
Look at two of them here. Between them they hold 2, 6, 7 and 8: four digits for two cells. Two of those go in, and two are left over for somewhere else.

Further down the same column sits a cell holding 6 and 7. Elsewhere in the same box sits a cell holding 2 and 8. Between them those two cells want exactly the four digits the crossing has, split evenly and with nothing shared.

Count it. Three cells of the column now take three different digits out of the four, and three cells of the box do the same. There is only one way the arithmetic works: 6 and 7 are used up inside the column, and 2 and 8 inside the box.
So nothing else in that column can be a 6 or a 7. Two cells lose one here.
The same argument runs the other way for the box. One pattern, two houses, two separate sets of eliminations, and no chain anywhere in it.
ALS-XZ
Two almost locked sets sharing a digit, and the elimination that follows.
The rule the hardest levels are built on. Everything above this stage is a variation of it.

An almost locked set is a group of cells in one house holding exactly one more digit than there are cells. Four cells with five digits between them. If it lost one digit it would be a locked set, hence the name.
Take two of them, sharing two digits. Call one of the shared digits the restricted one, and require that every place it appears in one set sees every place it appears in the other.
Then it can only be in one of the two sets. Whichever set does not get it becomes locked, which fixes the other shared digit inside it. And so any cell seeing that digit in both sets loses it.
Here is the elimination that comes out of it.
If this takes several readings, that is the normal number. Every technique past this point is this one wearing a different shape.
What the deep end asks
What changes at Insane and Nightmare, and why these levels need paper.
Everything up to here can be seen. You look at a row, a box, a pair of cells, and the answer is in front of you once you know the shape.
The two hardest levels are not like that. They ask you to follow an argument through three or four steps and hold all of it in your head at once, and almost nobody does that by looking.
So write it down. A pencil and the back of an envelope is not cheating and it is not a sign that you are bad at this. It is what everybody who solves these does.

The rules here are all the same idea: a group of cells one digit short of being full. Take that digit away and the group is forced, and a forced group makes the next one forced. That is the whole of the deep end.
Nothing below is a guess. Every step is proved, every hint will show you the proof, and if a puzzle here beats you, coming back to it in a week is the normal way it goes.
ALS-XY-Wing
Three groups in a chain, and the digit that cannot survive at either end.
Three groups this time, joined in a line: one at each end and one in the middle holding them apart.
Start with the two on the left. r3c9 holds 1 and 3. r1c8 holds 3 and 7. They share a box, so only one of them can be the 3.

Now the group down column 8: three cells holding 1, 3, 7 and 9 between them. Four digits, three cells, so it is one digit short of being full. It shares the 7 with r1c8, and every 7 in it is in that same column, so again only one side can take it.

Suppose one of the two marked cells in column 9 is a 1. It sees r3c9, so r3c9 is not 1, so it is 3. Then r1c8 is not 3, so it is 7. Then the group has no 7 left, so it is full, and it has to use 1, 3 and 9.
But those cells also see every 1 in the group, so the group cannot have a 1 either. The argument eats itself, and the 1 goes.
Two joins, three groups, and each step forces the next. Read it twice: it is a chain, and chains only make sense one link at a time.
Death blossom
One cell with a group waiting behind each of its digits.
This one has a shape you can see: a stem, and a petal for every digit the stem could be.
The stem is r1c4. It is a 5 or a 6, and nothing else. Two possibilities means two cases, and this technique deals with both at once.
Say it is a 5. Then r1c7, along the same row, holding 5 and 8, cannot be the 5. So it is the 8.

Say instead it is a 6. Look at these three cells in the same box: between them they hold 2, 6, 7 and 8. Four digits, three cells, one short of full. The stem sees all three, so its 6 takes the 6 away from them.
Now they are full, and three full cells use three digits: 2, 7 and 8. Only one of them can be the 8, so that is where the 8 goes.
Put the two cases together. Either there is an 8 at r1c7 or there is an 8 in that box, and there is no third case. Any cell that can see both places loses its 8, and two of them do.
Notice what you never had to know: which digit the stem actually is. Both roads end in an 8, so the answer does not depend on the fork.
Forcing chain
Take a cell both ways and see which way survives. The hardest thing in the app.
The last technique, and the only one that is not a pattern. There is nothing here to spot. There is only work.
This cell is a 2 or a 7. Everything else on the board has been squeezed dry, and nothing says which of the two it is.
So try one. Say it is a 2, in pencil, and follow only the easy consequences: a cell with one digit left, or a digit with one home left in its house.
They come quickly. A 2 is forced here, then a 7 there, then a 3, a 5, a 9. Keep going. Fourteen digits later, look at the marked cell.
It has nothing left. Every digit that could have gone there has been taken by something else. That is not bad luck, it is a contradiction, and it means the 2 was never possible at all.
So rub it all out and write the 7. Not because the 7 looks better, but because the 2 has been proved impossible, and two possibilities minus one leaves one.
This is proof by cases, and it is what people mean by working a puzzle out on paper. Use paper. Nobody holds fourteen forced digits in their head, and needing to write them down is not a weakness.
Now place it.
The other digit is the one that died. The 2 led to a cell with nothing in it, so what is left is the 7.
When nothing applies
Recheck before you guess, because a puzzle from this app always has a next step.
You will reach positions where you have looked at everything and found nothing. Here is what to do, and what not to.
What not to do is guess. Every puzzle in this app is solvable by reasoning, and a guess that happens to be right teaches you nothing while a guess that is wrong costs you the whole grid.

Recheck in this order. First, are all your notes true? A stale note is the most common cause of an impossible position, and this app will rub them out for you if you let it. Second, is a digit you placed actually right? Press hint and it will tell you.
Then look again for the cheap things. It is almost never a chain you missed. It is almost always a hidden single in a house you stopped looking at twenty moves ago.
What to look for first
Cheap patterns first, always, because they are common and they open the grid up.
You now know every technique this app can name. The last thing to learn is the order to look in.
Singles first, every time. Naked, then hidden. They are the most common by a wide margin and each one you place makes every other technique easier to find.
Then the cheap eliminations: pointing and claiming pairs. They are quick to check, house by house, and they often unlock a single straight away.
Then pairs and triples in the houses with the fewest empty cells. Then fish, then wings. Chains last, always, because they are the most work and the least common.

Hunting a Jellyfish before checking the singles is the sudoku equivalent of rewriting a program before reading the error message. The app grades puzzles by the hardest thing they need, but a Beyond is still mostly singles.
A Beyond, together
A hard puzzle is mostly easy steps with a few hard ones in it.
The last lesson. This is the grid the course has been walking through, at the Beyond grade, and here is the whole solve named technique by technique.
It opens with a naked single. Almost everything does.
Then a hidden single, in the box next door.
Now it stalls, and a pointing pair clears a column so the singles can start again. Notice that no digit was placed by that step and progress was made anyway.
A naked pair a little later, doing the same job in a house.
Deeper in, an X-Wing. By now the grid is half full and the notes are doing the work.
And near the end, the one that earns the grade: an ALS-XZ. One elimination, and the rest is singles again.
That is what Beyond means here. Not eighty one hard steps, but seventy easy ones and a handful that need everything you have learned.
